summary: Defines a common YANG module meant to be reused by various VPN-related modules, such as those for Layer 3 and Layer 2 VPN network models. It holds shared definitions so the other models stay consistent.

plainLanguage.summary:
Several YANG models describe VPNs: two for services and two for networks. They kept repeating the same definitions, and repeating definitions in one model made people think that model depended on the other.

RFC 9181 puts the shared definitions in one module, ietf-vpn-common, that any of the other models can import. The module defines no data of its own, only the identities, types and reusable groups that the others build on.

questions: what is the vpn common yang module
vpn route distinguisher assignment modes yang
subtitle: One shared YANG module of identities, types and groupings that every Layer 2 and Layer 3 VPN model can reuse.

tldr.problem: The YANG models for VPN services (L3SM, L2SM, L3NM, L2NM) all contain many of the same data nodes and structures, and copying them from one model into another made one model look as if it depended on another.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9181 defines a single module, ietf-vpn-common, holding reusable identities, types and groupings (VPN description, status, route targets, route distinguishers, ports, QoS classification and more) that any VPN module can import.
tldr.outcome: The module is used by the L3NM in RFC 9182 and is meant for the L2NM and for future revisions of the L3SM and L2SM. It defines no writable data nodes of its own.

today: RFC 9181 was published in February 2022 and is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the common module that the L3NM in RFC 9182 builds on.

sections.title: Why a Common VPN Module
sections.content:
The IETF has specified YANG modules for VPN services, among them the Layer 3 VPN Service Model (L3SM) in RFC 8299 and the Layer 2 VPN Service Model (L2SM) in RFC 8466. There are also network models: the Layer 3 VPN Network Model (L3NM) in RFC 9182 and the Layer 2 VPN Network Model (L2NM), which was still an Internet-Draft when this document was written.

These models share many data nodes and structures, at least in part. This document defines a common YANG module, ietf-vpn-common, to be reused by the other VPN-related modules, whether they describe Layer 2 or Layer 3 and whether they are network models or service models, including possible future revisions of the L3SM and the L2SM.

The module is written in YANG 1.1, its namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-vpn-common and its prefix is vpn-common. It uses types defined in RFC 6991, RFC 8294 and RFC 8519, and it uses the extension defined in RFC 8341.
sections.plainLanguage: Two of the models describe the service a customer buys and two describe how the network builds it. All four repeat the same definitions. This document gathers those shared definitions into one module that the others import, so that a model for Layer 3 networks does not have to depend on a model for Layer 2 networks.

sections.title: The Identities and Types the Module Defines
sections.content:
The module defines a set of identities, which are named constants that a configuration can refer to. Among them is service-type, which identifies the kind of VPN service, with values for L3VPN, VPLS using BGP, VPLS using the Label Distribution Protocol, Virtual Private Wire Service, BGP MPLS-Based Ethernet VPN, Ethernet VPN and Provider Backbone Bridging combined with Ethernet VPN. Another is vpn-signaling-type, which identifies how a service is signalled, with values for Layer 2 VPNs using BGP, LDP and the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol.

The module also covers the encapsulation features a VPN service may use: 802.1Q, QinQ, link aggregation and VXLAN. It names the routing features a service may run over: BGP, OSPF, IS-IS, RIP, Bidirectional Forwarding Detection and the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol, and the multicast protocols IGMPv1, IGMPv2, IGMPv3, MLDv1, MLDv2 and PIM. Both IPv4 and IPv6 identities are included.

Section 4 of the RFC gives the full list, which also covers address families, VPN topologies, network access types, operational and administrative status, the role of a site or node, service constraints, routing protocols, route import and export policies, bandwidth and Quality of Service.
sections.plainLanguage: The module defines a long list of named constants. They cover the kinds of VPN a provider can offer, the ways those VPNs can be signalled, the encapsulations and routing protocols they can run over, and the multicast protocols they can carry.

sections.title: The Reusable Groupings
sections.content:
A YANG grouping is a named bundle of data nodes that another module can insert wherever it fits. The common module provides these groupings.

  • vpn-description holds the administrative details of a VPN: an identifier, a name, a textual description and a customer name.
  • vpn-profile-cfg holds references to profiles that may be bound to a VPN, such as encryption, routing, forwarding, quality-of-service and Bidirectional Forwarding Detection profiles, plus external connectivity identifiers. The module does not define the structure of those profiles; it only names them so a VPN can be tied to them.
  • oper-status-timestamp and service-status carry the operational and administrative status of a VPN or one of its parts, and the time of the last change.
  • underlay-transport says how the underlay is set up, either as an abstract transport instance such as a VPN-plus instance, a virtual network identifier or a network slice name, or as a list of the actual protocols to enable, such as IP in IP, GRE, MPLS in UDP, Geneve, Segment Routing, RSVP with traffic engineering extensions, or BGP with labelled prefixes.
  • vpn-components-group groups VPN nodes, network accesses or sites so that diversity and redundancy rules can be applied per group.
  • placement-constraints says where a VPN node, network access or site may be placed.
  • ports defines source and destination port ranges or single port operators.
  • qos-classification-policy defines matching rules for classifying traffic, reusing the packet-fields groupings of RFC 8519. Only TCP and UDP are elaborated in this version.
sections.plainLanguage: Each grouping is a named set of fields that another model can drop in where it fits. There is one for a VPN's name and description, one for the profiles it may use, one for its status, one for its underlay, and others for grouping sites, for placement rules, for port ranges and for quality-of-service matching.

sections.title: Route Distinguishers and Route Targets
sections.content:
The vpn-route-targets grouping defines the Route Target import and export rules used in a BGP-enabled VPN. It works for Layer 3 VPNs as in RFC 4364 and for Layer 2 VPNs as in RFC 4664. Each entry has an identifier, a list of Route Targets and the type of those Route Targets, and the grouping also holds the import and export policy names.

The route-distinguisher grouping supports four assignment modes: direct assignment, full automatic assignment, automatic assignment from a named pool, and no assignment at all. It also covers deployments where only the Assigned Number part of a Route Distinguisher comes from a pool while the Administrator part is set to, for example, the Router ID of the VPN node. For that case there are three modes for the Assigned Number: explicit assignment, automatic assignment from a given pool, and full automatic assignment. The grouping also carries a read-only leaf holding the value the system assigned, so that a client can read back what was chosen.
sections.plainLanguage: Route Targets say which routes belong to a VPN and which can be imported or exported. A Route Distinguisher makes a VPN's routes unique in the operator's network. The module lets a client either supply the Route Distinguisher itself, ask for one from a named pool, ask the system to pick one, or say that none is needed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module defines a schema for data accessed over network management protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF. The lowest layer of NETCONF is a secure transport, and the one that must be implemented is SSH. The lowest layer of RESTCONF is HTTPS, and the one that must be implemented is TLS. The Network Configuration Access Control Model of RFC 8341 provides the means to restrict particular users to a preconfigured subset of the available operations and content.

The module by itself exposes no writable data nodes, no read-only state and no RPCs, so the RFC says there are no additional security issues to consider for it. Modules that use its groupings should identify their own security considerations. The RFC gives one example: reusing some of these groupings exposes privacy-related information such as customer-name, and disclosing it may violate the trust relationship between a provider and its customer.
sections.plainLanguage: The module holds no data of its own, so it adds no security risk on its own. The risk sits with the modules that import it, because some of the shared fields, such as the customer name, are private.

sections.title: Why the Models Do Not Copy Each Other
sections.content:
Appendix A of the RFC explains why the shared definitions ended up in their own module rather than being copied.

Early versions of the L3NM reused many of the data nodes defined in the L3SM, to avoid duplicating them and to ease passing data between the service layer and the network layer. That approach was abandoned, because the design was read as if deploying the L3NM depended on the L3SM, which is not the case. A provider may build its Layer 3 VPN services with the L3NM without exposing the L3SM to customers at all.

The same thing happened with the L2NM. Early versions reused data nodes from both the L2SM and the L3NM, and that was read as if deploying the L2NM required support for the L3NM. Appendix A shows an excerpt of the L2NM module importing ietf-l3vpn-ntw and using its service-status and svc-transport-encapsulation groupings.

A separate module of shared definitions avoids both problems: a model can reuse what it needs without appearing to depend on another model.
sections.plainLanguage: Earlier versions of the network models copied definitions from the service models to avoid writing them twice. That made readers think the network models needed the service models, which they do not. Putting the shared definitions in their own module removes the impression.
